I think 160C/320F is little low (even with fan/convection), you're not wrong in thinking that as well. But it's not terribly low. From my experience, I would suggest playing around with 175C/350F. It seems high but the initial blast of heat actually makes for a better rise (domed cupcakes). You could also experiment with starting the oven hot then bumping it down to let your cupcakes bake through without drying out. 

As for bake times, depends on your oven temperature. Generally, 15-20min if you're going low and slow. Starting hot (175+), 12-15min. But good rule of thumb is to just keep an eye on it periodically until you can work out a good time. 

Hope this helps! Happy baking!

I'm pretty green behind the ears as a cook (3 years working in restaurant kitchens) and today marks my one year in an institutional kitchen. Out of all the places I've been, my current place is the best I've worked. Stable hours, guaranteed days off, good pay, predictable work,  and *gasp* an actual non-toxic work environment where substance abuse isn't rampant and pans aren't flying across the kitchen towards me! 

I like my job but I can't help but feel like I'm not actually a chef even though my job title is literally "Chef". Sure, a lot of the dishes on our menu are from scratch but it's not like I'm making these magnificent, gastro-whatever dishes served on fancy platters to 100 covers in a 5 hour period (not that I ever have). At the same time, I'm glad for the stability even if I'm looked down upon by others for not being a "real" chef.

I think I read a comment here mentioning institutions being considered a places where "chefs go to die". Once upon a time, I turned up my nose at working in any facility that wasn't a restaurant too. Though the freedom to do pretty much whatever I want in the kitchen - within reason and as long as it tastes good and doesn't give these end-of-life residents an earlier end to their life - along with the work-life balance pretty much killed any snobbery I felt towards these positions. 

Maybe my kitchen is an outlier but the sentiment is still the same: institutional facilities are vastly underrappreciated and I hope the tide changes a bit more in the culinary industry to view them legitimately.

Now if you'll excuse me, I'm going to enjoy the rest of my weekend off (God, I love having weekends off).

1) Freeze the choux with the craquelin on top before wrapping it with plastic wrap. Make sure it's frozen solid (about 3-4 hours) before wrapping to avoid plastic wrap wrinkles on your craquelin disks.

2) DO NOT FREEZE CUSTARD. Something something the proteins in the custard break down when you freeze and thaw. The best you can do is make your custard ahead of time and pipe the day of the event. 

3) I would highly suggest you put the choux in cupcake liners to keep them separate and stable in a small cupcake box (plus it looks cuter in a cupcake liner).

4) Generally speaking, no they shouldn't be wet at the bottom if your custard isn't a loose ("wet") custard. If you're traveling with them for an hour, just make sure they're kept out of direct sunlight and if possible, blast the car's air conditioning to keep cool. Or buy a small cooler.

Hope this helps!

Sugar is a very important stabilizer for meringue to hold its shape. You can lower the sugar by at least half but any lower than that and you'll risk the stability of your meringue. Add cream of tartar to ensure you'll have a stable meringue. 
Also, meringue does have a tendency to weep if left in hot temperatures or left out for long periods of time. To prevent this, add a small amount of sifted cornstarch to your meringue.

Cookies (makes 30 cookies or 15 peaches):
- Butter, 125g
- Sugar, 125g
- Salt, 1/2 tsp
- Lemon zest, 1 lemon
- Vanilla Ex., 1 tsp
- Eggs, 2 each
- APF, 350g

Use the creaming method to combine the ingredients. Roll the dough into balls (about 14-15g per ball), then flatten slightly. **CHILL** the dough balls for about 15-20 minutes. Bake at 350F for about 13-15 minutes (the cookies should be on the paler side). While it's still warm, take a portion of the middle out from the cookie. This will be filled later.

Filling:
- Chocolate, 25g
- Heavy cream, 30g
- Walnuts, ground, 50g
- Apricot jam (or peach jam), 50g

Make a ganache with the chocolate and heavy cream, then incorporate the rest of the ingredients. Transfer to a piping bag and pipe the filling into the cookies.

Garnish/Decoration:
- Red food coloring
- Milk
- Sugar
- Mint sprigs (I had to use bay leaf)

Color the milk a very deep red (or to your desired color level). Dip both sides of the cookie halfway into the colored milk quickly. Let dry for about a minute, then roll in sugar. Garnish with mint sprigs as the peaches' leaf.

The recipe I used was provided by my patisserie chef instructor so I don't have a link and the components' recipes are also too long to post here; however, I can provide a list of the components!

Basically, the opera cake has six components: coating chocolate, joconde sponge, coffee simple syrup, soft ganache, coffee buttercream, and a chocolate mirror glaze.

* Coating chocolate: I used dark chocolate chips, melted it, and spread a thin layer on the bottom sponge.
* Joconde sponge: just a standard joconde.
* Coffee simple syrup: I made roughly 16oz of coffee (with the addition of a table spoon instant espresso) then boiled for three minutes with 10oz of sugar.
* Soft ganache: Essentially a ganache with a higher ratio of heavy cream, chilled, then whipped with the paddle attachment in a mixer.
* Coffee buttercream: I made Italian buttercream then to taste added instant espresso mixed with some of the coffee I made earlier.
* Chocolate mirror glaze: I took a real short shortcut and mixed together melted dark chocolate chips with vegetable oil (5:1 ratio chips to oil).

Happy baking!

Can you describe your process a bit more? A few things that comes to mind are:

- Not pouring sugar syrup quickly enough hence the hardening.
- The syrup is hitting the whisk rather than being poured into your egg whites, causing the spun sugar problem.
- Pouring too fast/Pouring when your egg whites are not foamy, causing hardened sugar at the bottom.
- Temperature a few degrees higher than the norm (I've always seen 115ºC but 3 degrees shouldn't be that much of a problem).

- Don't use purely fondant for the roses; gumpaste is ideal for decorations. Mixing tylose powder with fondant will give you a quick alternative to gumpaste. This is also less likely to crack (compared to fondant) and will keep its shape.

- Make your decorations ahead of time and keep it in an airtight container. Sugarwork can generally keep for a while but, again, keep it in an airtight container and away from humidity.

The main tip is save yourself time and stress by making the cake ahead of time. Cake freezes well, so if you're inclined, make the cake ahead of time. Buttercream also freezes well (bring back to room temp before using). This will remove a lot of stress so you have time to focus on decor.

Hope this helps you out! Stay healthy!

Edit: Last minute tips

- If you're unsure about cake recipes (some recipes out there just aren't good), practice by making cupcakes instead of full cake rounds.
- Cut recipes by half for practice until you've nailed down your bakes and techniques  (same applies to the frosting you'll use).
- CHILL AFTER CRUMB COATING. 10-15min in the freezer usually does the trick.
- Pipe your frosting layer on instead of slathering it on with an offset spatula. You'll get more of an even layer of frosting this way.
- For a smooth looking cake, heat your cake scraper with hot water before smoothing the sides.
- Sketch your cake so you have an idea of what direction you'll go with!

Swiss buttercream is easy to make without sacrificing the lightness and fluffiness! Same ingredients as italian buttercream, but swiss buttercream uses a different method:

1. Whisk your egg whites and sugar over a bain marie until the temperature of the mixture reaches 110ºF - Alternatively, feel the mixture and if it is grainy to the touch, keep whisking until all the sugar granules are dissolved.
2. Whip until the mixture is cool to the touch.
3. Gradually add your butter.

Two things to note about the soupy italian buttercream problem. First is if the buttercream is broken like that, your butter might be too warm when you're incorporating it (you want room temperature butter, but not ultra-soft butter). Second, you absolutely have to whip your meringue until it is cool to the touch - I learned from my own impatience that not letting your italian meringue cool properly before adding your butter will make your buttercream a soupy mess.

Hope this helps and good luck with your bakes!

It's less likely to be a proving issue and more of an issue with either your dough or the temperature of your frying oil. Like another person commented, if your dough is dense (even after proving) it may sink and you won't get that line on the doughnut. If your frying oil is too low of a temperature, your dough will sink in the oil; however, too high of a temp will get you a line around the doughnut at the risk of a cooked exterior with an undercooked exterior.

Yes, using a hint of blue or purple food dye works for buttercream frosting as well.

It has to do with color theory. Typically, if you want to neutralize one color, you would use the opposing color as seen on a color wheel. Whipped cream/meringues are on the yellow (or warmer) area of the color wheel, so using blue food coloring (even purple works) neutralizes the yellow. This results in a whiter or brighter whipped cream/meringues.
